Q: Which services are typically required to scale a LAMP stack for high-traffic production environments? A:

Redis (or ValKey, an open-source fork of Redis) is a great solution to reduce latency for specific cases, but you should be careful about how much you use it, because like every type of optimization, adding a cache increases complexity in your app.

For example, there's an old joke:

There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.

Cache invalidation means: how do you know when the data in cache needs to be refreshed with current data?

So while caching can be very beneficial, and might be the best way to solve certain performance problems in a given app, it creates its own issues too.

You might be interested in the chapter about caching in my upcoming book, More SQL Antipatterns.

Q: How can a class that implements an interface return another interface in a method? A:

Interfaces get implemented by classes, which are their subtypes. If you need an actual ISortStats, then you have to make a class that implements the ISortStats interface. If you need an ISorter, then you need a class that implements the ISorter interface. If the ISorter interface includes a method that returns an ISortStats, then it must do it by creating an instance of a class which implements ISortStats and returning it.

Q: Wait until service starts in bash-script A:

Try this.

local service_ready="LINE FROM JOURNAL INDICATING READY STATUS"
local last_service_invocation="$(systemctl show -p InvocationID --value MY_SERVICE.service)"

local tries=0
local max_tries=30

while ! journalctl _SYSTEMD_INVOCATION_ID="$last_service_invocation" | \
grep -qm1 "$service_ready"; do
    tries=$((tries+1))
    if (( $tries >= $max_tries )); then
        echo "Reached max tries: $max_tries"
        exit 1
    fi
    sleep 1
done

echo "Service ready."

If you have a simple type systemd service, it isn't necessarily ready when systemd shows it's active, so we have to parse the output like this.

This uses a newer feature of systemd to get journalctl output from only the most recent invocation of MY_SERVICE.service, and waits up to max_retries for service_ready to be in the output log.

With no timeout:

while ! journalctl _SYSTEMD_INVOCATION_ID="$last_service_invocation" | \
grep -qm1 "$service_ready"; do
    sleep 1
done

echo "Service ready."

Ideally, make a notify service

If you're looking for a better, more permanent solution, systemd is already designed to get status changes from services. You can add hooks in your application to send notifications to NOTIFY_SOCKET indicating status changes.

sd_notify() is the standard implementation for sending systemd notifications. The documentation also includes examples of writing messages to NOTIFY_SOCKET directly.

systemd-notify is a command line utility that wraps sd_notify(). You can use it to send these updates from an ordinary shell script. This may be useful if you are invoking an off-the-shelf application and you can't necessarily add hooks to send messages directly.

Make a unit file like this:

[Unit]
Description=My system service

[Service]
Type=notify
WorkingDirectory=/my/working/directory
User=myuser
ExecStart=/my/working/directory/start.sh
NotifyAccess=all
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

NotifyAccess=all is important to allow processes other than ExecStart (or other control processes) to notify systemd of state changes. all allows other processes we spawn in the script, like systemd-notify, to send notifications.

systemd-notify does attempt to send updates as its parent PID if it has sufficient privileges. That only worked for me as root.

systemd-notify will first attempt to invoke sd_notify() pretending to have the PID of the parent process of systemd-notify (i.e. the invoking process). This will only succeed when invoked with sufficient privileges. On failure, it will then fall back to invoking it under its own PID.

Here let's assume we're using myuser.

start.sh will be the new entrypoint for your service.

ACTUAL_SERVICE_EXEC="/path/to/actual/exec"
MY_LOG_FILE="/path/to/log/my_service.log"

notify_on_service_ready()
{
    echo "Waiting for my service to be ready..."

    local service_ready="LINE FROM LOG INDICATING READY STATUS"

    while ! grep -qm1 "$service_ready" "$MY_LOG_FILE"; do
        sleep 1
    done

    systemd-notify --ready
    echo "my service ready."
}

echo -n > "$MY_LOG_FILE"

notify_on_service_ready &

"$ACTUAL_SERVICE_EXEC" 2>&1 | tee "$MY_LOG_FILE"

First, truncate the log file to avoid a race condition where we read lines from a previous invocation.

This script creates a job calling notify_on_service_ready() that polls every 1 second for the service_ready line to appear in MY_LOG_FILE. Afterwards, it exits the while loop and sends the ready notification with systemd-notify.

The job runs in the background while the ACTUAL_SERVICE_EXEC is run, redirecting all output to both MY_LOG_FILE and stdout using tee. This retains the output in the systemd journal.

Now if you want to retrieve the service status from another script, you can simply check the active status of the service.

local tries=0
local max_tries=30

while ! systemctl is-active --quiet my_service; do
    tries=$((tries+1))
    if (( $tries >= $max_tries )); then
        echo "Reached max tries: $max_tries"
        exit 1
    fi
    sleep 1
done

echo "Service ready."

Q: How to list nodes from a custom mib file using snmpwalk? A:

I accidentally noticed that when I run snmpwalk without an OID, I get only 593 variables from my device, and the device-specific variables are missing. But if I add 1 as the OID, I get 2527 variables, including the ones which are the most useful. So in your case try adding 1 at the end of the snmpwalk command:

snmpwalk -v2c -c public localhost 1

Edit: The above method worked on an APC PDU, and on a Supermicro BMC. The BMC was a bit confusing because it did not use the OID names from the MIB file, but all the information I need is there.
